hero.name: Riya
hero.who: a second-year engineering student in Pune who keeps restarting her habits

story.b: Every Sunday night, Riya writes a perfect plan in her notebook. Wake at 5:30, run three kilometres, revise two chapters before college, no phone after ten. On Monday she follows all of it and feels unstoppable. On Tuesday she oversleeps by twenty minutes and skips the run. By Wednesday the notebook is under her pillow and the reels are back. Thursday night she tells her roommate Sneha that she just is not a disciplined person. Sneha laughs and points out that Riya has started this same plan six times since August. Riya laughs too, but it stings, because the exams are eight weeks away and she knows the problem is not the plan.

ask.q: Riya has quit the same big routine six times. What is the most useful thing for her to change first?
o: Write an even stricter plan so there is no room to slip
Shrink the plan to something so small she cannot fail at it
Wait until after the exams, when she will have more willpower
ask.why: A stricter plan asks for even more willpower, and willpower is exactly what runs out on Tuesday. Waiting changes nothing either. Shrinking the plan to a tiny daily action gives her something she can keep doing on a bad day, and that is where real change starts.

chapters.take: When a plan keeps failing, the plan is too big, not you too weak.

story.b: Riya drops the five-thirty alarm and the three kilometres. Her only promise is two pages of her weakest subject, thermodynamics, every night on the bus back from college. Two pages feels almost silly. The first week she reads them and forgets most of it. The second week she notices the formulas look familiar. By the fourth week she has covered a full unit without a single long study session, and she still has energy for lab work. Sneha asks how she suddenly got ahead. Riya shows her the bus ticket stubs she has been using as bookmarks, a small stack that keeps growing, one ride at a time.

ask.q: In week one Riya forgets most of what she reads. What should she do?
o: Keep the two pages going, because the gains show up only after weeks
Switch to a longer weekend session so it actually sticks
Stop, since two pages clearly makes no difference
ask.why: Small daily steps look useless at first because their effect is hidden. The value comes from stacking them for weeks. A long weekend session is easier to skip, and stopping in week one throws away the compounding before it begins.

chapters.take: Tiny daily actions look like nothing until the weeks add up.

story.b: Riya's class all want the same thing, a nine-pointer this semester. Last year Riya wanted it too and still scraped a seven. This time she stops staring at the target and looks at her week instead. She sets up a simple routine: two pages on the bus, ten practice problems after dinner, and a Sunday hour to fix whatever she got wrong. Some days she does not feel like it, so she does the smallest version. Midway through the term her friend Arjun is panicking because he has a big goal and no routine. Riya realises she has not thought about her final score in weeks, and her test marks have quietly gone up.

ask.q: Arjun has a big target and no routine. What would help him most?
o: Remind himself of the nine-pointer every morning
Set an even higher target to push harder
Build a small daily process he can follow even on bad days
ask.why: Everyone in the class has the same goal, so the goal alone does not decide who succeeds. A daily process does the actual work. Reminders and bigger targets add pressure but not progress; a routine he can repeat turns the goal into marks.

chapters.take: A goal says where you want to go. A system gets you there.

story.b: One evening Riya catches herself saying I am trying to study more, and it sounds weak even to her. She tries a different sentence: I am someone who studies a little every day. It feels strange, almost like pretending. But the next morning, waiting for the bus, she reaches for her notes instead of her phone, because that is what that kind of person would do. Each small choice becomes a tiny vote. She starts noticing the votes add up. By the end of the month, when friends invite her out on a weeknight, she says she will come after her ten problems, and she says it without feeling like she is giving anything up.

ask.q: Riya feels like she is pretending when she calls herself someone who studies daily. What should she do?
o: Drop the label until she has earned it with good grades
Keep acting like that person in small ways until the label feels true
Tell everyone so the pressure keeps her going
ask.why: A new identity feels fake at first because there is little proof yet. Each small action is proof. Waiting for grades skips the step that builds the belief, and public pressure fades fast. Small repeated actions make the label real.

chapters.take: Every small action is a vote for the person you want to be.

story.b: Riya notices that most of her lost evenings start the same way: she sits on her bed, the phone is right there, and forty minutes vanish. Instead of promising more self-control, she changes the room. The phone now charges in the hostel kitchen. Her thermodynamics book sits open on the desk with a pencil on top, so starting takes one second. She keeps a bottle of water next to it, because she studies longer when she is not getting up. Sneha jokes that Riya has rearranged her life around a charger. Riya does not mind. For the first time she studies without feeling like she is fighting herself the whole time.

ask.q: Arjun loses his evenings to his phone too. Which change will work best?
o: Delete social media for a week and hope it lasts
Promise himself he will only check it twice an evening
Keep the phone in another room and leave his books open on the desk
ask.why: Promises depend on willpower in the exact moment it is weakest. A one-week ban often ends in a binge. Changing where the phone lives and making the books the easy option lets the room do the work, so the good choice becomes the default.

chapters.take: Make the good habit easy to start and the bad one hard to reach.

story.b: Riya wants to add a short stretch to her day because her back hurts after long lab sessions. Instead of finding a new time for it, she ties it to something she already does without fail. After she pours her morning chai, she stretches for two minutes while it cools. Some days she does only one stretch, and that still counts. In the third week she gets a fever and misses two days in a row. She feels the old urge to give up the whole thing. Then she remembers her rule: one miss is normal, two in a row is where habits die. On the third morning she does a single stretch, and the chain starts again.

ask.q: Riya has missed her stretch two days in a row because of a fever. What should she do now?
o: Do even a tiny version today so the habit does not break
Restart properly next Monday with a fresh plan
Accept that she is not a morning-routine person
ask.why: Missing once is normal, but missing again and again is how a habit quietly ends. A tiny version today keeps the chain alive. Waiting for Monday is the old pattern that failed six times, and giving up turns one bad week into a story about who she is.

chapters.take: Missing once is normal. Do not let it turn into twice.

story.b: The exams arrive, and Riya is surprised by how calm she feels. She did not become a different person overnight. She read two pages on the bus, solved ten problems after dinner, kept her phone in the kitchen and stretched after her chai, most days and in tiny versions on bad ones. Her marks are the best she has had since school, but the bigger change is quieter. She no longer writes perfect Sunday plans. When she wants something new, she asks what the smallest daily version would be, and where in her day it can live. Sneha has started doing the same, and the hostel kitchen now has two phones charging every night.

chapters.take: Change comes from small habits kept, not big plans made.
